questions.topic: Why decimal fractions are not exact in binary floating point
questions.learningObjective: explain why adding two small decimals does not give the expected third
questions.practice: diagnosing a failed decimal sum in floating point
questions.stem: In double precision, 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004 rather than 0.3. Why?

options.text: Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 is stored exactly, so the sum inherits both rounding errors
The additions are carried out in a fixed point format keeping only a few digits
options.misconception: believes the arithmetic silently drops to a low precision format

options.text: The exponent range of double precision is too small for numbers this close to zero
options.misconception: blames the exponent range for a loss of significant digits

options.text: The sum is exact and only the comparison with 0.3 rounds the two sides differently
options.misconception: believes the arithmetic is exact and the equality test is at fault

questions.explanation: Double precision stores values as binary fractions, and one tenth has no finite binary expansion, so it is stored as the nearest available binary value, which is slightly under one tenth. Two tenths is stored slightly over two tenths. The addition of those two stored values is carried out exactly, but it inherits both storage errors, giving 0.30000000000000004, whose distance from the true three tenths is about 5.55 times 10 to the minus 17. Nothing to do with the exponent range is involved, since these numbers sit comfortably inside it, and the error is already baked in before any comparison is made.
questions.hint: Ask what the stored value of each decimal fraction actually is.

options.misconception: confuses the resolution of a format with its range

options.text: The smallest positive value the format can represent at all
options.misconception: confuses the relative resolution with the subnormal limit

options.text: The number of bits spent on the sign and the exponent together
options.misconception: believes epsilon reports the layout of the format

That is the finest relative resolution available near 1, and it is what sets the smallest relative change a stored number can register. It is not the range, which runs up to about 1.8 times 10 to the 308, and it is not the smallest representable positive value, which is a subnormal many orders of magnitude smaller than epsilon.
questions.hint: Ask how many representable values sit between 1 and the next one up.

questions.topic: Why catastrophic cancellation destroys significant digits
questions.learningObjective: explain why subtracting nearly equal quantities is dangerous
questions.practice: reasoning about a subtraction that loses accuracy
questions.stem: Why is subtracting two nearly equal computed quantities especially dangerous?

options.text: The rounding errors stay fixed while the answer shrinks, so the relative error explodes
Two large numbers of opposite sign always produce a negative zero result
options.misconception: believes cancellation always returns a negative zero

options.text: It only happens when the two numbers carry different exponents in the format
options.misconception: restricts cancellation to a particular case in the format

options.text: It changes the exponent of the result without disturbing the stored digits
options.misconception: believes cancellation corrupts the exponent field only

questions.explanation: Each of the two quantities arrives with an absolute rounding error of order epsilon times its own size. Subtracting cancels the leading digits, so the difference is much smaller than either input, while the two absolute errors do not shrink at all. Their ratio, and therefore the relative error of the difference, is the ratio of the input size to the result size, which can be enormous: computing (1 + 10 to the minus 10) minus 1 leaves about 8 correct digits out of the sixteen available. Nothing special happens to the exponent or the sign; the damage is entirely in the relative accuracy of a small result.
questions.hint: Ask how the rounding error compares with the size of the answer.

options.text: How far a relative perturbation of the input can be amplified in the output
How many arithmetic steps an algorithm needs to reach a given tolerance
options.misconception: confuses the difficulty of a problem with its sensitivity

options.text: How close the computed answer lies to the true answer in absolute terms
options.misconception: confuses a worst case bound with an achieved error

options.text: How badly a set of data degrades when stored in a coarser number format
options.misconception: confuses a property of the data with a property of the problem

questions.explanation: The condition number is the largest factor by which a relative change in the data can be magnified in the answer, so a condition number of 10 to the 12 says that an input known to 16 digits can leave only about 4 correct digits in the output. It is a property of the problem, not of the algorithm used, and it is a worst case: it bounds how bad things could be rather than reporting what actually happened. That distinction is why a large condition number is a warning about the problem rather than a measurement of the error already committed.
questions.hint: Ask how large a relative output error a small relative input error can produce.

questions.topic: Why Newton's method needs a derivative
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of the derivative in a Newton step
questions.practice: reasoning about the failure of a Newton step
questions.stem: Newton's method divides by the derivative at each step. Why is that division a source of danger?

options.text: Near a stationary point the derivative is tiny, so the step throws the iterate far away
The derivative is needed only to confirm that the function is increasing there
options.misconception: believes the derivative is a monotonicity check

options.text: Newton's method converges only when the function happens to be a polynomial
options.misconception: believes the method is restricted to polynomials

options.text: The derivative supplies the starting value, so no separate choice of start is needed
options.misconception: believes the derivative determines the starting point

questions.explanation: The step is the function value divided by the derivative, so wherever the graph is flat the denominator is small and the step becomes enormous, throwing the iterate far from the region where the linear approximation was any good. The standard example is the cubic with a single root near minus 1.769: started at 0 the method jumps to 1, then back to 0, then to 1 again, cycling forever. The derivative is required to form the tangent line, so it cannot be dropped, which is exactly why a method that needs no derivative, such as bisection, is preferred when no guarantee is wanted.
questions.hint: Look at what happens to the step size when the derivative is near zero.

questions.topic: Why bisection carries a guaranteed bound
questions.learningObjective: explain why bisection guarantees progress and a bounded error
questions.practice: reasoning about a bracketing method
questions.stem: Why does bisection keep a guaranteed bound on the error, when faster methods do not?

options.text: A sign change is preserved at every step, so the bracket halves and always holds a root
It converges quadratically, because each step is a full Newton step by another name
options.misconception: believes bisection inherits the fast local rate of Newton

options.text: It applies only to polynomials of low degree, where halving stays exact
options.misconception: restricts bisection to a class of functions it does not need

options.text: It requires the derivative, which is what makes the bound rigorous
options.misconception: believes a derivative is needed to prove a bracket shrinks

questions.explanation: Bisection needs only that the two endpoints straddle a sign change. Each step replaces the half of the interval that does not contain the crossing with the midpoint, so a sign change survives and the interval length is exactly halved, whatever the shape of the function. The root is therefore trapped between the endpoints at all times, and the error is at most half the interval length, giving the bound (b minus a) over 2 to the n plus 1 after n halvings. No smoothness, no derivative and no second crossing are needed, and that is why the guarantee is unconditional even though the rate is only linear.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the bracket when the answer is discarded.

questions.topic: Why Horner's method is cheaper than a full expansion
questions.learningObjective: state the computational advantage of Horner's method
questions.practice: comparing two ways of evaluating a polynomial
questions.stem: What makes Horner's method cheaper than expanding a polynomial before evaluating it?

options.text: It forms one intermediate result per coefficient instead of a whole power at each stage
It avoids addition altogether, using multiplication alone to reach the value
options.misconception: believes Horner trades additions for extra multiplications

options.text: It keeps the same operation count but rounds each intermediate result differently
options.misconception: believes Horner is the same work with different rounding

options.text: It squares the leading power repeatedly, reaching the value in a logarithmic count
options.misconception: confuses Horner with repeated squaring

questions.explanation: Expanding a degree n polynomial touches every power at every stage, needing n times n plus 1 over 2 multiplications, so 45 for degree 9. Horner rewrites the same expression as a single pass, needing n multiplications and n additions, so 9 for degree 9. The structural point is that Horner never forms any power of the variable at all; it keeps one running value and folds in the next coefficient each time, so the large intermediate quantities that the expanded form produces never appear. The savings are in work, and the extra accuracy is a separate and weaker claim.
questions.hint: Count the multiplications in each arrangement of the same terms.

questions.topic: What partial pivoting achieves in elimination
questions.learningObjective: describe the role of partial pivoting in Gaussian elimination
questions.practice: justifying a pivoting step
questions.stem: What does partial pivoting do when solving a linear system by Gaussian elimination?

options.text: It swaps in the largest available entry in the column, which keeps every multiplier small
It rearranges the rows so the matrix becomes diagonal before any elimination
options.misconception: believes pivoting performs the elimination itself

options.text: It selects the largest entries of the right hand side to become the new pivots
options.misconception: confuses the unknowns with the right hand side

options.text: It solves for the largest unknown first and back-substitutes for the rest
options.misconception: confuses a pivoting scheme with an ordering of unknowns

questions.explanation: Each multiplier is a ratio of an entry below the pivot to the pivot itself, so choosing the largest available entry in the column makes every such ratio at most 1 in size. Small multipliers mean the updated entries cannot blow up during elimination, which is what keeps the rounding errors introduced along the way from being amplified into the answer. The scheme is called partial because it picks the best candidate only within the current column, not across the whole remaining submatrix, which is a weaker but far cheaper choice.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the multipliers when the pivot is tiny.

questions.topic: What a large growth factor warns about
questions.learningObjective: interpret the growth factor of an elimination step
questions.practice: reading a diagnostic from an elimination run
questions.stem: Elimination produces intermediate entries much larger than the original matrix. What does that warn you?

options.text: Rounding errors in those large entries are amplified into the solution, so the bound is weak
The matrix is singular, since no pivot could be found in that column
options.misconception: believes growth is a symptom of singularity

options.text: The elimination was carried out with no rounding at all, hence the large values
options.misconception: believes growth implies exact arithmetic

options.text: The system has a condition number below one, which no matrix can have
options.misconception: believes growth implies a condition number under one

questions.explanation: The growth factor is the ratio of the largest entry appearing anywhere during elimination to the largest entry of the original matrix. Entries that grow mean that every rounding error made while those entries were being formed is itself large, and the back substitution then divides by pivots of comparable size, so those errors survive into the answer nearly undiminished. A growth factor near 1, which partial pivoting usually delivers, means the intermediate entries stayed in the original range and the error bound is correspondingly tight. Growth alone says nothing about whether the system has a solution.
questions.hint: Compare the largest intermediate entry with the largest original entry.

questions.topic: What the power method converges to
questions.learningObjective: state what the power method converges to and when
questions.practice: describing the limit of repeated matrix multiplication
questions.stem: Repeatedly multiplying a starting vector by a matrix, and rescaling each time, converges to what?

options.text: The eigenvector of largest eigenvalue magnitude, provided that one clearly dominates
The eigenvector of smallest magnitude, since that direction grows most slowly
options.misconception: believes the slowest growing direction is the limit

options.text: The sum of all the eigenvalues, which is the trace of the matrix
options.misconception: believes repeated multiplication accumulates a trace

options.text: The dominant eigenvector only when the matrix is negative definite throughout
options.misconception: believes the method needs negative definiteness

questions.explanation: A matrix splits any vector into components along its eigenvectors, and each component is multiplied at every step by the eigenvalue along that direction. The component with the largest eigenvalue magnitude therefore grows fastest relative to the others, and after normalisation it swallows the rest, leaving the direction of that eigenvector. The catch is that the dominance must be clear: if two eigenvalues are nearly equal in magnitude, or the largest is negative and close in size to the second largest, the direction keeps swinging and the iteration does not settle. The rate of approach is governed by the ratio of the second largest eigenvalue to the largest.

questions.topic: What the Rayleigh quotient gives
questions.learningObjective: state the property that makes the Rayleigh quotient a cheap eigenvalue estimate
questions.practice: reasoning about a Rayleigh quotient
questions.stem: For a real symmetric matrix, what can be said about the Rayleigh quotient of a vector?

options.text: It lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues and equals them at eigenvectors
It always equals the trace of the matrix divided by the dimension of the matrix
options.misconception: believes the quotient is independent of the vector

options.text: It is the largest eigenvalue whenever the vector has any nonzero entry at all
options.misconception: believes any usable vector reveals the top eigenvalue

options.text: It equals the determinant of the matrix, whatever vector is put into it
options.misconception: believes the quotient depends only on the matrix

questions.explanation: For a symmetric matrix the Rayleigh quotient is a weighted average of the eigenvalues, with weights set by how much of the vector lies along each eigenvector, and the weights are non-negative and sum to one. This is what makes the quotient a cheap and safe estimate: combined with the power method, which improves the direction, each iterate yields a value that is at least as good as the direction warrants.
questions.hint: Try it on an eigenvector, then on a vector that is not one.

questions.learningObjective: explain why forming the normal equations squares a condition number

options.text: The new matrix is always singular whenever the original matrix is square

options.text: The right hand side grows by exactly the dimension of the original matrix
options.misconception: believes the reformulation inflates the right hand side

The reformulation is attractive because the matrix becomes square and symmetric, but the price is paid in exactly the digits the computation was supposed to deliver.

questions.topic: What the standard error of a Monte Carlo estimate is

questions.stem: The function f of x equal to x cubed minus 2x plus 2 has exactly one real root, and it lies between minus 2 and 0. What is that root?

questions.explanation: A condition number of 1e12 says that a relative perturbation of the data of size 1e-16 could be amplified into a relative error of size 1e-4 in the worst case, so at most about 12 of the 16 available digits are at risk. It does not say that any particular run lost them, and the achieved error is usually far smaller, often limited by ordinary rounding at the 1e-16 level. Concluding a specific error from the condition number mistakes a ceiling for a measurement, which is the same error as reading a worst case as an average.
questions.hint: Ask whether a worst case bound is the same statement as a measurement.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Cancellation belongs to the data and the formula, not the algorithm
questions.learningObjective: explain why cancellation is a property of an expression rather than a coding fault
questions.practice: explaining the limits of an algorithm against the limits of a problem
questions.stem: Explain why a cancelling subtraction is a property of the data and of the formula being evaluated, and not a fault in the algorithm that evaluates them.

answer.exemplar: The two quantities being subtracted each arrive with an absolute rounding error of order epsilon times their own size, and those errors are unrelated to each other, so they do not cancel. Subtracting nearly equal numbers produces a result much smaller than either input, while the two errors stay at the size of the inputs, so the relative error of the result is roughly the size of the inputs divided by the size of the result. That ratio is a property of the numbers themselves: no choice of algorithm changes it, because a correctly rounded subtraction of two stored values is already the best any algorithm can do with those two stored values. The classic illustration is forming the exponential of a small number minus one, where the function value and 1 agree to some number of digits and the subtraction throws those shared digits away, so the result of order 10 to the minus 8 keeps only about 8 of the 16 available digits. Working in a higher precision, or rescaling the argument, or using a function written to compute the small quantity directly all recover the digits, and all of them change the arithmetic being performed rather than the data. The distinction worth keeping is between a backward error, which is what the algorithm is allowed to introduce, and a forward error, which is amplified by the problem: when the problem is ill conditioned the forward error is large no matter how careful the algorithm, and the honest response is to reformulate or to state the limitation rather than to write more careful code.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to argue that correctly rounded operations cannot help, quantify the amplification as the input size over the result size, and name reformulating the expression or raising the working precision as the actual remedies.
questions.hint: Compare the size of the rounding error with the size of the answer it lands in.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why the normal equations square a condition number
questions.learningObjective: explain the squaring of the condition number under the normal equations
questions.practice: explaining why a reformulation loses digits
questions.stem: Explain why forming the normal equations squares the condition number of a least squares problem, and what to do instead.

answer.exemplar: The condition number measures how far the solution can move when the data move, and it is built from the singular values of the design matrix, which record how much the matrix stretches in different directions. Forming the normal equations replaces that matrix by its transpose times itself, and the singular values of a product are the products of the singular values, so the new singular values are the squares of the old ones. Ratios of singular values are therefore squared too, and the condition number comes out squared. Since a condition number is a decimal exponent in the number of digits lost, squaring it doubles the loss: a design matrix with a condition number of 1e8 gives normal equations with one of 1e16, which in double precision spends the entire budget of 16 digits before the arithmetic begins, leaving nothing. The alternative is never to form the product. Applying a factored or orthogonal transformation to the design matrix, then solving the triangular system and transforming back, uses the original singular values throughout, so the conditioning is unchanged and 8 digits of headroom remain. The normal equations are tempting because they turn a rectangular system into a square symmetric one, but the symmetry is not worth the digits it costs.

questions.explanation: A model answer must connect the squared condition number to the squared singular values, translate that into a concrete loss of digits, and then name the factored or orthogonal route as the alternative that avoids forming the product.
questions.hint: Ask what the singular values of a matrix times its transpose are.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: Why bisection is guaranteed and Newton is not
questions.learningObjective: explain the contrast in guarantees between a bracketing and a tangent method
questions.practice: explaining convergence guarantees and orders
questions.stem: Explain why bisection carries an unconditional error bound while Newton's method does not, and what the order of convergence of a method means.

answer.exemplar: Bisection carries a piece of information that cannot be lost: that a sign change is still bracketed between its two endpoints. Whatever the shape of the function, the half of the interval that does not contain the crossing can be discarded, so the interval shrinks by exactly a factor of 2 at every step and the root stays inside it. The error is therefore at most half the interval width at all times, which is a guarantee about every possible function with a sign change and no smoothness required. Newton carries no such certificate. It replaces the function by its tangent at the current iterate, and the tangent's intercept can land anywhere at all: if the derivative is small the step is huge, and if the tangent is a poor local approximation the step can move away from the root entirely. The cubic with a single root near minus 1.769, started at 0, cycles between 0 and 1 forever. The order of convergence describes how the error shrinks, and a method has order p with constant c if the next error is about c times the current error raised to the p. Bisection has order 1 with c equal to one half, which is why the halving is exact. Newton has order 2, so each step roughly squares the current error and the number of correct digits doubles each time, but only once the iterates are close enough for the tangent to be a good approximation. The secant method drops the derivative in favour of a difference quotient and settles at order 1.618, between the two. So a higher order is a statement about speed near the root, and a bound is a statement about safety everywhere, and a method can have one without the other.

questions.explanation: A model answer should distinguish the invariant that bisection preserves, a bracketed sign change, from the local approximation Newton relies on, and should define the order of convergence before comparing the rates 1, 1.618 and 2.
questions.hint: Ask what information each method carries from one step to the next.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_2
questions.topic: What a condition number says and does not say about accuracy
questions.learningObjective: state the scope and the limits of what a condition number reports
questions.practice: explaining the reach of a conditioning diagnostic
questions.stem: Explain what a condition number does and does not tell you about the accuracy of a computed answer.

answer.exemplar: A condition number is the largest factor by which a small relative change in the data can be magnified in the answer, so it tells you how much of the accuracy present in the input can survive. Multiplying it by the size of the perturbation in the data bounds the relative error of the answer, and that is the number to quote when asked how many digits are at risk. Three things it does not tell you are worth naming. It is a worst case, so the error actually achieved is usually far smaller, and quoting the condition number as the error overstates the damage. It says nothing about the algorithm: the same problem solved carefully and solved carelessly can both be governed by the same condition number, which is why a stable algorithm and a fragile one give visibly different answers from the same data. And it is a property of the problem, not of the data alone, so no amount of extra data precision rescues an ill conditioned formulation: doubling the input precision buys at most one digit when the condition number is 1e12. The practical consequence is that a large condition number is a reason to change the formulation, for instance to avoid forming a product that squares the conditioning, or to report an interval of uncertainty rather than a single misleading digit string. What it cannot do is certify an answer as accurate, because a small condition number permits large errors from a badly chosen algorithm and a large one does not force them.

questions.explanation: A model answer must state that a condition number amplifies input perturbations, then separate the three things it does not report: the achieved error, the quality of the algorithm, and any rescue from higher input precision.
questions.hint: Separate a ceiling on amplification from a measurement of what happened.
